main.title: Metal Slug
main.subtitle: A tank with a life of its own
main.summary: Nazca’s hand-drawn run-and-gun adventure sends Marco and Tarma through six missions full of soldiers, prisoners and expressive machinery.

cards.heading: Marco, Tarma and the Slug
cards.text: Metal Slug is Nazca’s side-scrolling run-and-gun game, first released for the Neo Geo arcade system in Japan on 19 April 1996. Marco Rossi and Tarma Roving cross six missions against General Morden’s rebel army, firing at soldiers and much larger machines. One or two players can advance together, finding new guns, throwing grenades and rescuing prisoners along the route. The small tank that gives the game its name can be boarded along the way, adding another layer to a campaign already crowded with moving characters and destructible scenery.

cards.heading: Getting into the vehicle
cards.text: Entering the Metal Slug changes both attack and survival. Its weapons offer greater firepower, while the vehicle absorbs damage that would cost the soldier a life on foot. The player can move between these states as the stage demands, using the tank until it is time to leave it behind. Freed prisoners reward a rescue with supplies, and keeping the rescued total through the end of a mission earns extra points. Losing a life resets that tally, tying careful play to the people saved along the way.

cards.heading: A battlefield full of reactions
cards.text: Much of the game’s personality appears in the moments around the shooting. Soldiers cook, talk or relax before noticing the player; machines recoil and collapse through elaborate animation. The scenery can break apart to reveal items, encouraging shots into the surroundings as well as directly at enemies. Several members of Nazca had worked on Irem action games, bringing that experience into a more immediately approachable set of controls. The expressive drawings make the battlefield readable through reactions, turning small enemies and the squat tank into memorable performers.

main.title: The Legend of Oasis
main.subtitle: Before the golden armlet changed hands
main.summary: The Legend of Oasis is Ancient's action role-playing adventure, first released for Saturn in Japan on 26 April 1996.

cards.heading: Before the golden armlet changed hands
cards.text: The Legend of Oasis is Ancient's action role-playing adventure, first released for Saturn in Japan on 26 April 1996. Known as The Story of Thor 2 in Europe, it takes place before Beyond Oasis and follows Leon, a pupil entrusted with the Golden Armlet. He must gain the loyalty of six elemental spirits and oppose Agito, the bearer of the Silver Armlet. Direct fighting and environmental puzzles share an overhead world, with the spirits providing the abilities that gradually turn its barriers into routes through the adventure.

cards.heading: Six spirits in the surroundings
cards.text: Leon summons a spirit by sending a Spirit Ball towards an object, with the object determining which companion appears. Water, fire, earth, sound, darkness and air each have their own spirit and practical uses. A companion may fight, heal Leon or help solve a puzzle, so noticing the surroundings becomes part of choosing what to summon. The expanded group builds on the earlier game's central idea: an elemental ability belongs to the landscape as well as the hero, and finding the correct place to call it is part of the solution.

cards.heading: Weapons with another use
cards.text: Short swords, long swords and bows provide different attacks, with directional and button combinations producing special moves. Arrows can also activate switches, making equipment useful beyond an immediate enemy. This combination encourages the player to approach a room as both a fighting space and a small mechanical problem. Yuzo Koshiro produced the game and composed its music, with Ayano Koshiro contributing its art. The sharper Saturn presentation gives Leon's movements and surroundings greater detail while preserving the close connection between physical action, summoned companions and obstacles that defined the earlier adventure.

main.title: Jumping Flash! 2
main.subtitle: Robbit looks down on another world
main.summary: Jumping Flash! 2 is Exact and MuuMuu's PlayStation platform game, first released in Japan on 26 April 1996. The robotic rabbit Robbit searches for MuuMuus scattered across large three-dimensional stages by Captain Kabuki. As in the original, the player sees through Robbit's eyes, using enormous jumps to explore structures from above. Height becomes a practical way to understand a level. An object difficult to locate from the ground can reveal itself during the ascent, turning the next landing into a decision made while the player is still far above it.

cards.heading: Robbit looks down on another world
cards.text: Jumping Flash! 2 is Exact and MuuMuu's PlayStation platform game, first released in Japan on 26 April 1996. The robotic rabbit Robbit searches for MuuMuus scattered across large three-dimensional stages by Captain Kabuki. As in the original, the player sees through Robbit's eyes, using enormous jumps to explore structures from above. Height becomes a practical way to understand a level. An object difficult to locate from the ground can reveal itself during the ascent, turning the next landing into a decision made while the player is still far above it.

cards.heading: Use the view between jumps
cards.text: Robbit's triple jump gives access to distant platforms and high vantage points. The player studies the ground while airborne, choosing where to land and which part of the stage to investigate next. A meter makes the availability of that jump clearer, while a longer draw distance helps more of the world remain visible. These refinements support the original's unusual relationship between movement and observation. The player is not simply crossing a gap: each ascent offers another chance to assemble a useful picture of the places and targets spread below.

cards.heading: Refine an early three-dimensional platform game
cards.text: Koji Tada directed the sequel, with Takeo Miratsu returning to compose its music. Much of the earlier interface was retained, allowing development to focus on new worlds and improvements to the existing play. Reviews welcomed the graphics and handling while questioning the short length and close resemblance to the first game. North American and British editions followed later in 1996. The sequel demonstrates how distinctive the original idea already was, developing a first-person platform game around the pleasure of rising above a landscape and choosing a route back down.

main.title: Inti Creates
main.subtitle: A studio specialising in 2D action
main.summary: Inti Creates was founded on May 8, 1996.

cards.heading: Founded in Japan in 1996
cards.text: Inti Creates was founded in Japan on May 8, 1996. Its later work ranged from Mega Man Zero and Mega Man ZX to original projects such as Azure Striker Gunvolt and Blaster Master Zero. Across different hardware generations, the studio developed a particular focus on two-dimensional action, detailed character animation and responsive controls.

cards.heading: Animation and responsive control
cards.text: Working across different machines required the studio to adapt to changing screen sizes, resolutions, palettes, memory formats and input devices. Clear animation and reliable collision detection were especially important when action filled a small display. The team's projects repeatedly depended on players recognising an attack and responding through a character's movement.

cards.heading: Mega Man Zero on Game Boy Advance
cards.text: Mega Man Zero brought the series' action to Game Boy Advance. Its compact screen gave particular importance to sprite size, the distance at which danger became visible and the clarity of attacks. Aggressive movement, close combat and sharp animation gave the game a demanding pace within those limits.

cards.heading: Tagging targets in Gunvolt
cards.text: Azure Striker Gunvolt changes the rhythm of a run-and-gun game by letting players tag targets, then damage them continuously with electricity. Position, movement and energy management shape how that attack is sustained. The player has to coordinate the initial shots with the electrical ability while responding to surrounding dangers.

main.title: Fire Emblem: Genealogy of the Holy War
main.subtitle: Two generations in the same war
main.summary: Nintendo released Fire Emblem: Genealogy of the Holy War for Super Famicom in Japan on May 14, 1996.

cards.heading: The campaign spans two generations
cards.text: Nintendo released Fire Emblem: Genealogy of the Holy War for Japan's Super Famicom on May 14, 1996. Intelligent Systems expanded the scale of its maps and divided the campaign between two generations. Relationships and marriages in the first half influence the children who fight later, passing equipment and abilities into a new army. The war's history becomes part of the party the player builds.

cards.heading: Crossing larger battlefields
cards.text: Large maps connect castles, roads and groups of units across entire regions. Moving cavalry, organising formations and choosing which position to capture all affect the progress of a battle. Traversing these longer fronts requires planning beyond the next encounter, as units can be needed in several places during the same campaign.

cards.heading: Relationships and inheritance
cards.text: Relationships between first-generation characters influence the children who join the second half. Parents affect equipment, statistics and inherited skills. Choosing which characters spend time together can therefore shape a later party as well as the current battle. The system links the development of personal relationships to longer-term decisions about the army.

cards.heading: An army shaped by its parents
cards.text: The second generation encounters a world changed by its parents' actions. Familiar rules now apply to new characters carrying inherited weapons and traits. The player can recognise earlier decisions in the composition and equipment of this later army, connecting the two halves of the story through the units used in combat.

main.title: Keio Flying Squadron 2
main.subtitle: Rami steps into the foreground
main.summary: Keio Flying Squadron 2 is Victor Entertainment's Saturn sequel, first released in Japan on 17 May 1996.

cards.heading: Rami steps into the foreground
cards.text: Keio Flying Squadron 2 is Victor Entertainment's Saturn sequel, first released in Japan on 17 May 1996. Rami Nanahikari returns in a comic treasure hunt, but the adventure now centers on platforming with shooting sections woven into it. That shift brings the heroine closer to the player: running, jumping and interacting with objects occupy the foreground between the airborne passages. Animated scenes continue the series' playful presentation, making its exaggerated characters and unusual version of historical Japan central to the journey.

cards.heading: A platform adventure with flying passages
cards.text: The change of genre grew from the team's wish to show the characters more prominently through larger sprites. Platform stages give Rami a physical presence that differs from the first game's constant flight, while the shooter sections preserve a connection to that earlier adventure. Moving between the two changes the rhythm of the journey. The player alternates between reading the shape of the ground and responding to an advancing screen, with the same cast and visual humor connecting those different demands.

cards.heading: Keeping animation at the center
cards.text: Development began in 1994 as an enhanced Sega CD project before moving to Saturn and becoming a full sequel. The team retained two-dimensional play as three-dimensional games became more prominent. Studio Pierrot again produced the animated scenes, and Tsukasa Tawada composed the music. A European release followed in September 1996. The project shows a studio using a more powerful machine to enlarge an established illustrated world, making the characters and their animation the reason for changing how the adventure plays.

main.title: Quake
main.subtitle: Fast movement through three-dimensional worlds
main.summary: id Software’s 1996 shooter placed fast movement and combat in fully three-dimensional environments.

cards.heading: Deciding what the player might see
cards.text: Quake's fully three-dimensional environments required more than replacing flat enemies with models. Programmer Michael Abrash describes a world divided into spatial regions, with tools calculating which regions might be visible from each other. During play, the engine could use that prepared information to avoid considering much of the hidden level. John Carmack's approach spent work before the game ran in order to save work during a frame. The resulting speed depended on how the level was organised as well as on the drawing code itself.

cards.heading: Speed moves work into the tools
cards.text: Abrash also records the cost of that decision for the people building maps. Calculating visibility could take long enough to interrupt a designer's iteration, even on powerful equipment. Near release, Carmack tried a different visibility method that promised tighter results. It improved some scenes but made the worst cases slower, so it did not replace the shipping approach. The change was judged against the scenes in which performance was already most difficult.

cards.heading: The program becomes inspectable
cards.text: A later source release made the engine available to study and modify. In id Software's README, John Carmack explained that the program was released under the GNU General Public License, including source-sharing obligations for distributed modifications. The original game data retained its existing copyright and licence. The release also credited Dave Kirsh and Robert Duffy with preparing the source code.

cards.heading: Quake reaches the PC
cards.text: id Software released Quake to the public on PC on June 22, 1996. Levels, monsters, projectiles and the viewpoint inhabit a continuous three-dimensional space. Its fast movement, multiplayer and modding possibilities helped establish a lasting community around the game. The engine also became a foundation that developers could study, modify and build upon.

cards.heading: Finding the exit through a three-dimensional level
cards.text: In Quake's single-player mode, players explore levels, facing monsters and finding secret areas before reaching an exit. Switches or keys open doors, and reaching the exit takes the player to the next level. Before accessing an episode, there is a set of three pathways with easy, medium, and hard skill levels. The fourth skill level, "Nightmare", was described by the game manual to be "so bad that the entry is hidden, so people won't wander in by accident". The game has no dedicated "use" key; players instead physically push against objects to activate them.

cards.heading: Strafe-jumping and rocket-jumping
cards.text: The gameplay in Quake was considered unique for its time because of the different ways the player can maneuver through the game. The player can start and stop moving suddenly, jump unnaturally high, and change direction while mid-air. Bunnyhopping or strafe-jumping grant faster movement, while rocket jumping enables the player to reach otherwise-inaccessible areas at the cost of some health. Many of these non-realistic behaviors contribute to Quake's appeal. Multiplayer Quake was one of the first games singled out as a form of electronic sport. A notable participant was Dennis Fong, who won John Carmack's Ferrari 328 at the Microsoft-sponsored Red Annihilation tournament in 1997.

cards.heading: Trent Reznor and the sound of Quake
cards.text: Quake's music and sound design was done by Trent Reznor and Nine Inch Nails, using ambient soundscapes and synthesized drones to create atmospheric tracks. In an interview, Reznor remarked that the Quake soundtrack "is not music[;] it's textures and ambiences and whirling machine noises and stuff. We tried to make the most sinister, depressive, scary, frightening kind of thing... It's been fun." The game includes an homage to Reznor in the form of ammo boxes of nails for the Nailgun and Super Nailgun decorated with the Nine Inch Nails logo.

main.title: Nintendo 64
main.subtitle: Learning to move through space
main.summary: Nintendo 64 makes movement through 3D worlds tactile, and brings four players together around one television.

cards.heading: 1996 / Bringing three dimensions home
cards.text: Nintendo 64 reached Japan on 23 June 1996, with Super Mario 64 among its first games. Nintendo's partnership with Silicon Graphics, announced in 1993 as Project Reality, had become a home console built around three-dimensional worlds. Beneath the case, its CPU and Reality Coprocessor worked together, sharing the same main memory. The circuit board makes that collaboration tangible: a small collection of chips had to turn geometry, textures, sound and player input into a world that responded immediately.

cards.heading: A controller for moving through space
cards.text: Three grips gave the controller its unusual silhouette. Players could hold its left and right handles for the directional pad, or move one hand to the centre for the analogue stick and the trigger underneath. Super Mario 64 made the stick's range easy to understand: a gentle tilt could produce a careful walk, while a stronger push sent Mario running. The change was felt through the hands, as movement through space became something to judge continuously rather than choose one direction at a time.

cards.heading: The cartridge shapes the game
cards.text: Nintendo kept games on cartridges while PlayStation and Saturn used CDs. Fast access to a cartridge's data suited play with little waiting, but its smaller capacity and higher manufacturing costs brought different constraints. Recorded voices, film sequences and large collections of images all competed for space. Developers compressed material, built scenes from reusable elements or generated more of the presentation in real time. The opened Game Pak shows the physical choice behind those decisions: a game stored on chips rather than an optical disc.

cards.heading: Four players, one television
cards.text: Four controller sockets were built into the front of the console. Friends did not need a separate multitap to join a four-player game. Mario Kart 64 divided the television between racers, while its battle arenas made the same shared screen a place to hunt one another. The original packaging pictured the split-screen modes alongside the races. Playing together meant watching your own corner, hearing the people beside you and knowing that everybody could also see what you were doing.

cards.heading: 64DD / Drawing, building and sharing
cards.text: The 64DD attached beneath the console and reached Japan in 1999. Its rewritable magnetic disks offered a different purpose from the familiar cartridge: players could save creations as well as play finished games. Mario Artist explored drawing, modelling and animation, and the Randnet service connected the system to an online network. The package also included the Expansion Pak, increasing the console's main memory from 4 MB to 8 MB. Few disks reached shops, but the hardware preserves an unusual branch of Nintendo 64's story, with making and sharing placed beside playing.

main.title: Pilotwings 64
main.subtitle: Nintendo / Paradigm Simulation · Nintendo 64
main.summary: Pilotwings 64 is Nintendo and Paradigm Simulation's Nintendo 64 flying game, released alongside the console in Japan. Six pilots attempt licence tests using a hang glider, rocket belt and gyrocopter, with additional activities unlocked through progress. Islands contain landmarks, targets and routes that look inviting from above. The immediate objective may be a sequence of rings or a careful landing, but the scenery also encourages the player to look around. Learning a machine gives a different way to explore the same small world.

cards.heading: Learn to fly above a miniature world
cards.text: Pilotwings 64 is Nintendo and Paradigm Simulation's Nintendo 64 flying game, released alongside the console in Japan. Six pilots attempt licence tests using a hang glider, rocket belt and gyrocopter, with additional activities unlocked through progress. Islands contain landmarks, targets and routes that look inviting from above. The immediate objective may be a sequence of rings or a careful landing, but the scenery also encourages the player to look around. Learning a machine gives a different way to explore the same small world.

cards.heading: The landing belongs to the whole flight
cards.text: Tests score more than reaching a destination. Time, accuracy, damage and the quality of a landing can all affect the result, making the final approach something to prepare before the target fills the screen. The hang glider uses air currents, the rocket belt can hover and adjust its thrust, and the gyrocopter requires room to take off and land. Each form of flight asks the player to develop another sense of momentum while reading the same landscape for useful reference points.

cards.heading: A launch game that leaves room to look
cards.text: Good results open further tests and bonus events, while Birdman mode allows freer exploration in a bird suit. A miniature United States supplies recognisable landmarks alongside playful Nintendo details. Dan Hess's score accompanies the different activities, helping establish a calmer character than the console's other major launch adventure. Pilotwings 64 demonstrates three-dimensional space through the pleasure of becoming comfortable inside it: the better the player understands the aircraft, the more attention can be given to the world passing beneath it.

main.title: Super Mario 64
main.subtitle: Learning how to move all over again
main.summary: An analog stick and an adjustable viewpoint made running in three dimensions a subject of its own.

cards.heading: Room to practise in three dimensions
cards.text: Super Mario 64 accompanied the Nintendo 64's Japanese launch in 1996. Its spaces gave players room to practise movement, judge depth and discover different objectives within the same landscape.

cards.heading: The camera becomes part of control
cards.text: A 3D world also created a new design problem: the camera. Positioning a viewpoint could help or obstruct a jump, so seeing became part of controlling. The game helped establish a widely influential vocabulary, while leaving a problem that later designers would continue to revisit.

cards.heading: A jump needs room for error
cards.text: Shigeru Miyamoto recalled that judging jumps became more difficult when Mario moved into three dimensions. Earlier games had allowed designers to measure a jump in pixels; depth was harder for players to estimate. Late in Super Mario 64's development, the team adjusted the levels to accept jumps that came sufficiently close, allowing more room for error.

cards.heading: Movement before the courses
cards.text: The development interviews describe a prototype in which Mario and Luigi moved around a room. The analogue stick controlled movement and a button changed the camera. The team wanted that basic activity to feel enjoyable before adding courses and enemies. Work on the viewpoint proceeded alongside terrain and depth calculations so the player could see the spaces through which the character moved.

cards.heading: Several players, one view
cards.text: Discussing Super Mario 3D World in 2013, Yoshiaki Koizumi described using a camera that maintained a set distance and direction. Multiplayer brought another requirement: the team rejected split-screen and developed a shared view that could keep the players together. The camera's behaviour followed the needs of several characters moving through the same course.

cards.heading: Camera control becomes optional
cards.text: Kenta Motokura noted that a single player could also use a free-camera mode controlled through the Wii U GamePad's gyro sensor. Koizumi presented it as an option for experienced players seeking a greater sense of immersion. Satoru Iwata distinguished that extra control from the actions needed to finish a course, allowing players to use the additional camera freedom when they wanted it.
